antidotes.stem: A 30-year-old is brought in after a large bupropion XL overdose and has a generalised tonic–clonic seizure. Oxygenation and glucose are normal.
antidotes.explain: Benzodiazepines are **first-line for seizures** caused by bupropion toxicity; treat recurrent seizures with escalating anticonvulsant therapy and supportive care.
wrong: Phenytoin is generally ineffective for toxicological seizures and may worsen dysrhythmias.
It reverses benzodiazepines, not bupropion toxicity, and can precipitate seizures.
It reverses opioid toxicity, not bupropion-induced seizures.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE; Goldfrank’s Toxicologic Emergencies, 11th ed.

antidotes.stem: A patient presents after a citalopram overdose with recurrent torsades de pointes and a prolonged QT interval. They remain conscious between episodes.
antidotes.explain: IV **magnesium sulfate** is the acute treatment for torsades de pointes, even if the serum magnesium is normal.
wrong: Calcium is not the treatment for torsades caused by QT prolongation.
This is used for sodium-channel blockade with QRS widening, not isolated QT prolongation.
Adenosine treats selected supraventricular tachycardias, not torsades.
antidotes.source: AHA ACLS 2020; TOXBASE: Citalopram overdose

antidotes.stem: A patient has taken a large carbamazepine overdose and remains markedly drowsy, with a rising serum concentration and no ileus or bowel obstruction. The airway is protected.
antidotes.explain: Carbamazepine undergoes **enterohepatic recirculation**; multiple-dose activated charcoal can enhance elimination in significant poisoning when the airway is protected.
wrong: It does not reverse carbamazepine toxicity and may provoke seizures.
Whole-bowel irrigation as the sole measure
It may be considered in selected cases, but multiple-dose activated charcoal is the specific enhanced-elimination treatment here.
This does not meaningfully enhance carbamazepine elimination.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE: Carbamazepine overdose; AACT/EAPCCT position statement on multiple-dose activated charcoal

antidotes.stem: After a lamotrigine overdose, a patient develops hypotension and a markedly widened QRS complex on ECG. There is no evidence of hyperkalaemia.
antidotes.explain: Sodium bicarbonate is used for suspected **sodium-channel blockade with QRS widening** in severe lamotrigine poisoning.
wrong: Magnesium is used for torsades, not QRS widening from sodium-channel blockade.
Calcium treats selected calcium-channel blocker toxicities and hyperkalaemia, not this ECG effect.
It does not reverse lamotrigine toxicity and may precipitate seizures.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE: Lamotrigine overdose; Goldfrank’s Toxicologic Emergencies, 11th ed.

antidotes.stem: A patient with a quetiapine overdose remains hypotensive after initial fluid resuscitation. ECG shows sinus tachycardia without QRS widening.
antidotes.explain: If hypotension persists after fluids, **noradrenaline** is an appropriate vasopressor for quetiapine-associated vasodilatory hypotension.
wrong: Beta-blockade may worsen hypotension and is not indicated for sinus tachycardia in this setting.
It is not routine treatment for quetiapine overdose and may cause serious adverse effects.
There is no QRS widening to indicate treatment for sodium-channel blockade.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE: Quetiapine overdose

antidotes.stem: Following a massive ibuprofen overdose, a patient develops severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis and haemodynamic compromise. The airway and circulation are being supported.
antidotes.right: IV sodium bicarbonate for severe metabolic acidosis
antidotes.explain: There is no specific antidote; **IV sodium bicarbonate** may be used to correct severe, clinically significant acidaemia alongside supportive care.
wrong: It is an antidote for paracetamol poisoning, not ibuprofen toxicity.
Urinary alkalinisation to enhance ibuprofen clearance
Alkalinisation is not an established method to enhance ibuprofen elimination.
It has no role in NSAID poisoning.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE: Ibuprofen overdose

antidotes.stem: A patient presents after an extended-release venlafaxine overdose and has a generalised seizure. Point-of-care glucose and oxygenation are normal.
antidotes.explain: Treat venlafaxine-related seizures promptly with a **benzodiazepine** and provide supportive airway and cardiorespiratory care.
wrong: Phenytoin is generally not recommended for seizures caused by drug poisoning.
It does not treat venlafaxine toxicity and may precipitate seizures.
It is not an antidote for venlafaxine-induced seizures.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE: Venlafaxine overdose; Goldfrank’s Toxicologic Emergencies, 11th ed.

antidotes.stem: During a regional anaesthetic, a patient develops a seizure followed by ventricular arrhythmia shortly after receiving bupivacaine. Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity is suspected.
antidotes.explain: For severe **local anaesthetic systemic toxicity**, administer 20% lipid emulsion alongside resuscitation and seizure control.
wrong: Used for sodium-channel blocker toxicity, not as the specific rescue treatment for bupivacaine toxicity.
Does not reverse local anaesthetic systemic toxicity.
Reverses opioid toxicity, not bupivacaine toxicity.
antidotes.source: ASRA Checklist for Treatment of Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity, 2020

antidotes.stem: A patient accidentally takes a large daily dose of methotrexate instead of the prescribed weekly dose and develops mucositis and pancytopenia. The serum methotrexate concentration is elevated.
antidotes.explain: Leucovorin bypasses the folate blockade and is the key **rescue treatment** after methotrexate toxicity; dosing is guided by the exposure and clinical context.
wrong: It is not an adequate substitute for leucovorin rescue in significant methotrexate toxicity.
This is an antidote for fluoropyrimidine toxicity, not methotrexate.
Used for methaemoglobinaemia, not antifolate toxicity.
antidotes.source: NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service, Managing interactions with methotrexate; EXTRIP Workgroup, Methotrexate recommendations

antidotes.stem: A patient with end-stage kidney disease accidentally takes a large amount of gabapentin and becomes deeply obtunded, requiring mechanical ventilation. Gabapentin is predominantly renally eliminated.
antidotes.explain: In severe gabapentin poisoning with **impaired kidney function**, extracorporeal removal is suggested; provide supportive care as well.
wrong: Gabapentin is not a benzodiazepine, and flumazenil will not reverse its effects.
Naloxone does not reverse gabapentin toxicity.
Activated charcoal as the sole treatment
It does not address severe established toxicity or impaired drug clearance.
antidotes.source: EXTRIP Workgroup, Gabapentin and Pregabalin recommendations, 2022

antidotes.stem: A patient with advanced chronic kidney disease develops coma and respiratory depression after taking a therapeutic dose of baclofen. The presentation is attributed to baclofen accumulation.
antidotes.explain: EXTRIP suggests extracorporeal treatment for **baclofen toxicity in kidney impairment**, particularly when coma requires mechanical ventilation.
wrong: Baclofen acts at GABA-B receptors; flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.
This does not reverse baclofen toxicity.
It is not an antidote for baclofen poisoning.
antidotes.source: EXTRIP Workgroup, Baclofen recommendations, 2021

antidotes.stem: A patient taking haloperidol develops painful torticollis and sustained upward eye deviation shortly after a dose increase. They are alert and have no fever or autonomic instability.
antidotes.explain: This is an **acute dystonic reaction**; a parenteral anticholinergic such as benztropine rapidly relieves symptoms.
wrong: Used for malignant hyperthermia and sometimes neuroleptic malignant syndrome, not uncomplicated acute dystonia.
Used in neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which is not the presentation here.
Can help akathisia, but is not the preferred rapid treatment for acute dystonia.
antidotes.source: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th edition

antidotes.stem: A patient who overdosed on phenelzine is severely agitated, tachycardic and hypertensive, without evidence of end-organ injury. They are being managed in a monitored resuscitation area.
antidotes.explain: Benzodiazepines are first-line for agitation and sympathetic overactivity in **MAOI poisoning**; use supportive care and manage persistent severe hypertension with specialist guidance.
wrong: It is not an antidote for MAOI poisoning and may cause serious adverse effects.
Oral activated charcoal as the only treatment
It does not control agitation or cardiovascular complications and may be unsafe in an unprotected airway.
Beta-blockade alone can be hazardous in severe sympathomimetic toxicity.
antidotes.source: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11th edition

antidotes.stem: After an increase in risperidone, a patient develops intense inner restlessness and an inability to sit still. There is no rigidity, fever or clonus.
antidotes.explain: For antipsychotic-induced **akathisia**, propranolol is a commonly recommended symptomatic treatment, alongside reviewing the causative drug.
wrong: More useful for acute dystonia or parkinsonism than akathisia.
Used for malignant hyperthermia and sometimes neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Used in selected cases of serotonin toxicity, not antipsychotic-induced akathisia.
antidotes.source: American Psychiatric Association, Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Schizophrenia, 3rd edition

antidotes.stem: A patient presents early after a large colchicine overdose, with severe vomiting and abdominal pain. The ingestion is potentially life-threatening, but the patient is currently haemodynamically stable.
antidotes.right: Urgent toxicology consultation and supportive care; no established specific antidote
antidotes.explain: There is **no routinely available specific antidote** for colchicine poisoning; early specialist advice and intensive supportive management are essential.
wrong: This is used as rescue for methotrexate toxicity, not colchicine poisoning.
It does not reverse colchicine toxicity.
It is not a specific treatment for colchicine poisoning.
antidotes.source: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11th edition

antidotes.stem: A patient with a methadone overdose develops recurrent torsades de pointes with marked QT prolongation. Their circulation is currently stable between episodes.
antidotes.explain: Give **IV magnesium sulfate** for torsades, even if the serum magnesium is normal. Correct contributing electrolyte abnormalities and stop QT-prolonging drugs.
wrong: Calcium is not the first-line treatment for torsades unless there is a separate indication such as hypocalcaemia.
This is used for sodium-channel blockade with QRS widening, not isolated QT prolongation and torsades.
Amiodarone can further prolong the QT interval and worsen torsades.
antidotes.source: AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC, Adult Advanced Life Support; TOXBASE, Methadone poisoning

antidotes.stem: A patient is deeply sedated with respiratory depression after taking a large amount of buprenorphine. Repeated standard doses of naloxone produce little improvement.
antidotes.explain: Buprenorphine’s high receptor affinity may require **larger naloxone doses**; a continuous infusion may be needed because its effects can outlast naloxone. Provide ventilatory support.
wrong: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioid toxicity, and can provoke seizures in some overdoses.
Atropine does not reverse opioid-induced respiratory depression.
Physostigmine is not an opioid antidote and may cause serious adverse effects.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE, Buprenorphine poisoning; Goldfrank’s Toxicologic Emergencies, 11th ed.

antidotes.stem: A benzodiazepine-naive adult is found drowsy after an isolated accidental diazepam overdose. They have respiratory depression, and there is no evidence of dependence, seizure disorder or co-ingestion.
antidotes.explain: In a **selected isolated benzodiazepine overdose**, flumazenil can reverse sedation and respiratory depression. Avoid it when dependence, proconvulsant co-ingestion or seizure risk is present.
wrong: Naloxone reverses opioid toxicity, not benzodiazepine effects.
Physostigmine is not used to reverse benzodiazepines and may cause seizures or arrhythmias.
Flumazenil is not appropriate in all overdoses; it can precipitate withdrawal or seizures in high-risk patients.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE, Benzodiazepine poisoning; BNF, Flumazenil

antidotes.stem: A patient with advanced kidney failure becomes comatose and hypoventilates after taking a therapeutic baclofen dose. The drug is renally cleared, and supportive care has not improved the encephalopathy.
antidotes.explain: Baclofen is dialysable; **haemodialysis is suggested for toxicity with coma requiring mechanical ventilation, particularly with impaired kidney function**. Continue supportive care.
wrong: Naloxone does not reliably reverse baclofen toxicity.
Flumazenil does not reverse baclofen and may introduce seizure risk.
This is not an effective method to enhance baclofen elimination.
antidotes.source: EXTRIP Workgroup, Baclofen poisoning recommendations, Kidney International 2021

antidotes.stem: A patient with a clozapine overdose remains severely hypotensive despite IV fluids. There is no evidence of anaphylaxis or another cause of shock.
antidotes.explain: Use **norepinephrine** for persistent clozapine-associated hypotension. Avoid epinephrine where possible because clozapine’s alpha-blocking effect can produce paradoxical worsening of hypotension.
wrong: Alpha-receptor blockade may cause epinephrine to worsen hypotension through unopposed beta-2 vasodilation.
Flumazenil does not reverse clozapine toxicity.
Physostigmine is not a treatment for clozapine-induced shock and can cause serious complications.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE, Clozapine poisoning

antidotes.stem: A patient develops a generalised seizure after a tramadol overdose. The seizure is ongoing, and there is no evidence of hypoglycaemia or another immediately reversible cause.
antidotes.explain: Treat tramadol-associated seizures promptly with an **IV benzodiazepine** such as lorazepam or diazepam, while supporting airway and breathing.
wrong: Phenytoin is generally ineffective for toxicological seizures and may worsen some poisonings.
Flumazenil can precipitate seizures and does not treat tramadol toxicity.
Naloxone may be considered for opioid-related respiratory depression, but it is not the first-line anticonvulsant.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE, Tramadol poisoning; BNF, Status epilepticus

antidotes.stem: A child becomes markedly drowsy with bradycardia and hypotension after swallowing clonidine tablets. Airway and ventilatory support are being provided.
antidotes.right: Supportive care with close airway and haemodynamic monitoring
antidotes.explain: There is **no established specific antidote** for clonidine poisoning; management is supportive, with airway support and treatment of clinically significant bradycardia or hypotension as needed.
wrong: Atropine may be considered for symptomatic bradycardia but does not reverse clonidine toxicity.
Naloxone as a reliably curative antidote
Naloxone has inconsistent benefit and should not replace supportive care.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE, Clonidine poisoning

antidotes.stem: After a sertraline overdose, a patient develops agitation, diaphoresis, tremor and inducible clonus despite initial supportive measures. They can swallow safely and have no contraindication to enteral medication.
antidotes.explain: For clinically significant serotonin toxicity, **cyproheptadine** may be used as an adjunct to supportive care and benzodiazepines; it is given enterally because no parenteral formulation is available.
wrong: Dantrolene is used for malignant hyperthermia and is not the standard antidote for serotonin toxicity.
Bromocriptine is sometimes used in neuroleptic malignant syndrome and may worsen serotonin toxicity.
Flumazenil does not treat serotonin toxicity and can provoke seizures in overdose.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE, Serotonin syndrome; BNF, Cyproheptadine

antidotes.stem: A patient with chronic lithium exposure presents with polyuria, hypernatraemia and very dilute urine consistent with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. They are haemodynamically stable and can take oral medication.
antidotes.explain: **Amiloride** reduces lithium entry into collecting-duct cells via epithelial sodium channels and is commonly used for lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
wrong: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is due to renal resistance to vasopressin, so desmopressin is usually ineffective.
It does not block lithium entry into collecting-duct cells as amiloride does.
Acetazolamide is not the usual targeted treatment for lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
antidotes.source: BNF, Amiloride; UpToDate, Lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus

antidotes.stem: A patient who took a large amount of sustained-release morphine initially responds to naloxone but repeatedly becomes apnoeic as the naloxone wears off. They require repeated rescue doses.
antidotes.explain: For recurrent respiratory depression after a long-acting opioid, use a **naloxone infusion** after effective reversal, with ongoing respiratory monitoring because toxicity may recur.
wrong: Activated charcoal as the only treatment
Charcoal does not promptly reverse established respiratory depression and must not delay airway support or naloxone.
Long-acting opioid effects can outlast naloxone, creating a risk of recurrent respiratory depression.
antidotes.source: BNF, Naloxone; TOXBASE, Morphine poisoning

antidotes.stem: A 32-year-old presents after swallowing a large quantity of naproxen tablets. They have nausea and epigastric pain but normal observations, renal function and acid–base status.
antidotes.right: Supportive care; there is no specific antidote.
antidotes.explain: Naproxen overdose is managed with **supportive care**, including assessment and monitoring for complications. No specific antidote is available.
wrong: This is used for paracetamol poisoning, not naproxen overdose.
Urinary alkalinisation is used for salicylate poisoning, not routine NSAID overdose.
This chelator is used for significant iron poisoning.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE; BNF, NSAID poisoning

antidotes.stem: A patient is brought to the emergency department after an intentional ingestion of a large quantity of celecoxib. They are alert and haemodynamically stable, with no evidence of co-ingestants.
antidotes.right: Supportive care and observation; no specific antidote.
antidotes.explain: There is **no specific antidote** for celecoxib overdose. Management is guided by symptoms and includes observation and supportive treatment.
wrong: This may reverse benzodiazepine effects in selected cases, not celecoxib toxicity.
This reverses opioid toxicity, not NSAID toxicity.
This is used in selected cases of local anaesthetic systemic toxicity, not celecoxib overdose.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE; BNF, celecoxib

antidotes.stem: A 40-year-old is found deeply comatose with hypotonia and respiratory depression after taking a large amount of baclofen. They require intubation and ventilatory support.
antidotes.right: Supportive care, including airway and ventilatory support.
antidotes.explain: Baclofen overdose can cause profound CNS depression; treatment is primarily **supportive**, with close monitoring and respiratory support as needed. There is no established specific antidote.
wrong: It does not reverse baclofen toxicity and may provoke seizures in some poisonings.
It reverses opioid effects, not baclofen toxicity.
It is not an antidote for baclofen-induced coma.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE; EXTRIP Workgroup, baclofen poisoning recommendations

antidotes.stem: A young adult presents after ingesting a large quantity of methylphenidate and is severely agitated, tachycardic and hypertensive. They have no hyperthermia or seizure at assessment.
antidotes.right: Benzodiazepines for agitation and sympathetic overactivity.
antidotes.explain: Benzodiazepines are first-line to control **agitation and adrenergic excess** in stimulant toxicity; provide supportive care and monitor for complications.
wrong: Isolated beta-blockade is not first-line and may worsen vasoconstriction through unopposed alpha activity.
This treats opioid toxicity, not methylphenidate toxicity.
This reverses benzodiazepines and has no role in methylphenidate poisoning.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE; BNF, methylphenidate

antidotes.stem: A teenager presents after taking a large overdose of atomoxetine and develops marked agitation, tachycardia and a generalised seizure. Airway and breathing are currently maintained.
antidotes.explain: Treat seizures from atomoxetine toxicity with **benzodiazepines** and provide supportive care, including monitoring of cardiovascular status.
wrong: It is generally not the preferred first-line treatment for toxicological seizures.
It does not reverse atomoxetine toxicity.
It is not an antidote for atomoxetine and can precipitate seizures in susceptible patients.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE; BNF, atomoxetine

antidotes.stem: A patient is brought in after a large ingestion of dextromethorphan and is markedly agitated with nystagmus and ataxia. They are maintaining their airway and have no features of opioid respiratory depression.
antidotes.right: Supportive care, with benzodiazepines if agitation is severe.
antidotes.explain: Dextromethorphan toxicity is managed with **supportive care**; benzodiazepines can be used for severe agitation or seizures. Naloxone is not routine in the absence of respiratory depression.
wrong: This is used for paracetamol poisoning, not dextromethorphan.
It does not reverse dextromethorphan toxicity.
This is used for selected sodium-channel-blocking drug toxicities, not routine dextromethorphan poisoning.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE; BNF, dextromethorphan

antidotes.stem: A patient who has taken a very large amount of loperamide develops recurrent torsades de pointes with marked QT prolongation. They remain unstable despite initial magnesium and electrical treatment.
antidotes.right: Isoprenaline or temporary overdrive pacing, with specialist toxicology advice.
antidotes.explain: Loperamide can cause life-threatening QT prolongation and torsades. For recurrent episodes, **increase the heart rate** with isoprenaline or overdrive pacing, alongside standard resuscitation.
wrong: This is not an antidote for loperamide-related arrhythmia.
It does not treat the prolonged QT mechanism or recurrent torsades.
It may further prolong the QT interval and worsen torsades risk.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE; Resuscitation Council UK, Adult Advanced Life Support guidance

antidotes.stem: Immediately after a rapid high-dose intravenous fentanyl administration, a patient develops severe chest-wall rigidity and cannot be ventilated effectively. Oxygenation is deteriorating.
antidotes.right: Naloxone, with neuromuscular blockade and ventilation if needed.
antidotes.explain: Fentanyl-induced rigidity can impair ventilation. **Naloxone** reverses opioid effects; severe cases may require neuromuscular blockade and assisted ventilation.
wrong: It does not reverse opioid-induced chest-wall rigidity.
This is used for selected sodium-channel-blocking toxicities, not fentanyl rigidity.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE; BNF, fentanyl

antidotes.stem: After a massive mefenamic acid overdose, a patient develops a generalised seizure. Their airway is secured, and the seizure persists despite an initial benzodiazepine dose.
antidotes.right: Give further intravenous benzodiazepine treatment and manage in a resuscitation setting.
antidotes.explain: Seizures in mefenamic acid poisoning are treated with **benzodiazepines**, with airway support and toxicology consultation. There is no specific antidote.
wrong: This does not treat seizures caused by mefenamic acid.
It is not an anticonvulsant and may provoke seizures.
This is used for iron poisoning, not NSAID-induced seizures.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE; BNF, mefenamic acid

antidotes.stem: A patient with normal baseline renal function is brought in after an isolated pregabalin overdose. They are drowsy but maintaining their airway, with stable observations and no co-ingestants identified.
antidotes.right: Supportive care and observation; no specific antidote.
antidotes.explain: Isolated pregabalin overdose is managed with **supportive care** and monitoring for CNS and respiratory depression. There is no specific antidote.
wrong: It does not reverse pregabalin and may cause harm in mixed or uncertain overdoses.
It is not an antidote for pregabalin toxicity.
This is used for paracetamol poisoning, not pregabalin overdose.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE; BNF, pregabalin

antidotes.stem: An adult is brought in after ingesting a large quantity of phenazopyridine tablets and develops cyanosis, chocolate-brown blood and a low pulse-oximeter reading that does not improve with oxygen. Co-oximetry confirms significant methaemoglobinaemia.
antidotes.explain: Methylene blue is the **specific treatment** for clinically significant drug-induced methaemoglobinaemia. Check for **G6PD deficiency**, which increases the risk of haemolysis and poor response.
wrong: Used for some drug-induced sodium-channel blockade, not methaemoglobinaemia.
The antidote for paracetamol poisoning, not phenazopyridine-induced methaemoglobinaemia.
Used for selected cases of local anaesthetic systemic toxicity, not this presentation.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE: Phenazopyridine; UK MHRA: Methylene blue—risk of haemolytic anaemia in G6PD deficiency

antidotes.stem: A patient presents after a large phenobarbital overdose with coma and respiratory depression despite initial supportive care. The serum concentration remains high and the clinical course is prolonged.
antidotes.explain: For **severe long-acting barbiturate poisoning**, extracorporeal treatment is recommended; **intermittent haemodialysis** is preferred when available. Continue supportive care and consider multiple-dose activated charcoal if the airway is protected.
wrong: Not recommended as the specific enhanced-elimination strategy for severe phenobarbital poisoning.
Reverses benzodiazepine effects and may precipitate seizures; it does not reverse phenobarbital.
Reverses opioid toxicity, not barbiturate toxicity.
antidotes.source: EXTRIP Workgroup: Recommendations for the use of extracorporeal treatments in poisoning with barbiturates (2021)

antidotes.stem: A young adult is brought in after a large doxylamine overdose with severe agitation, delirium, mydriasis and dry skin. The ECG shows a narrow QRS, and there is no history of seizure or chronic tricyclic antidepressant use.
antidotes.explain: With severe **anticholinergic delirium** and no ECG contraindication, physostigmine can reverse central toxicity. Give it with cardiac monitoring and expert oversight; avoid it when **QRS is widened** or tricyclic poisoning is suspected.
wrong: Reverses opioid toxicity, not doxylamine-induced delirium.
Indicated for significant sodium-channel blockade with QRS widening, which is absent here.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE: Doxylamine; American Academy of Clinical Toxicology / European Association of Poisons Centres and Clinical Toxicologists: Physostigmine position statement

antidotes.stem: A patient with a severe phenobarbital overdose is drowsy but has a protected airway and stable haemodynamics. The ingestion was several hours ago, and the drug concentration remains elevated.
antidotes.explain: Phenobarbital undergoes **enterohepatic recirculation** and is adsorbed by charcoal; multiple doses can enhance elimination in significant poisoning. Use only when the airway is protected and bowel function is adequate.
wrong: A single dose does not provide the enhanced elimination sought in significant phenobarbital poisoning.
Not the preferred enhanced-elimination method for phenobarbital.
Does not reliably enhance phenobarbital elimination and risks fluid and electrolyte complications.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE: Phenobarbital; EXTRIP Workgroup: Recommendations for the use of extracorporeal treatments in poisoning with barbiturates (2021)

antidotes.stem: A 24-year-old presents 10 hours after a deliberate acetaminophen overdose. The serum concentration is above the treatment line on the nomogram, and liver tests are currently normal.
antidotes.explain: N-acetylcysteine replenishes **glutathione** and is indicated when the concentration is above the treatment line; give it even if liver tests are initially normal.
wrong: Used for selected sodium-channel-blocker toxicity, not acetaminophen poisoning.
Used for toxic alcohol poisoning, not as the standard antidote here.
antidotes.source: NICE Clinical Guideline CG145, Self-harm: longer-term management (acetylcysteine for paracetamol poisoning); MHRA acetylcysteine guidance

antidotes.stem: A patient who overdosed on amitriptyline is hypotensive and has a broad-complex tachycardia with a QRS duration of 160 ms.
antidotes.explain: Sodium bicarbonate treats **cardiac sodium-channel blockade**, narrowing the QRS and improving hypotension in tricyclic antidepressant toxicity.
wrong: Used for calcium-channel-blocker toxicity or hyperkalaemia, not TCA-induced QRS widening.
Used for torsades de pointes, not the primary treatment for this toxicity.
Can precipitate seizures in TCA overdose and is not indicated.
antidotes.source: AHA Focused Update on the Management of Patients With Cardiac Arrest or Life-Threatening Toxicity Due to Poisoning, 2023

antidotes.stem: A patient is found unresponsive with slow, shallow respirations, pinpoint pupils and a history of injecting heroin. Bag-mask ventilation is started.
antidotes.explain: Naloxone reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression; **support ventilation first** and repeat or infuse naloxone if respiratory depression recurs.
wrong: Treats symptomatic bradycardia or cholinergic toxicity, not opioid respiratory depression.
antidotes.source: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care, 2020; WHO, Community Management of Opioid Overdose, 2014

antidotes.stem: A patient taking warfarin presents with an intracerebral haemorrhage and an INR of 6.2. Rapid reversal is required.
antidotes.right: Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate plus intravenous vitamin K
antidotes.explain: Four-factor PCC rapidly replaces vitamin K-dependent clotting factors; **intravenous vitamin K** sustains reversal as the infused factors are cleared.
wrong: Reverses warfarin more slowly and requires a larger infusion volume than PCC.
antidotes.source: NICE NG24, Blood transfusion; ACC Expert Consensus Decision Pathway on Management of Bleeding in Patients on Oral Anticoagulants, 2020

antidotes.stem: A patient taking dabigatran develops a life-threatening gastrointestinal bleed; the last dose was taken two hours ago and renal function is impaired.
antidotes.explain: Idarucizumab is a specific monoclonal antibody fragment that binds and reverses **dabigatran** rapidly.
wrong: Reverses factor Xa inhibitors, not dabigatran.
Reverses vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin.
antidotes.source: European Heart Rhythm Association Practical Guide on the Use of Non-Vitamin K Antagonist Oral Anticoagulants, 2021

antidotes.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes who accidentally took excess glibenclamide has recurrent severe hypoglycaemia despite intravenous dextrose.
antidotes.explain: Octreotide suppresses pancreatic insulin release and prevents **recurrent sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia** after initial correction with dextrose.
wrong: May raise glucose briefly but can stimulate further insulin release and does not reliably prevent recurrence.
Reverses opioid toxicity, not sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia.
antidotes.source: AACT/EAPCCT Position Paper: Octreotide for sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia, Clinical Toxicology, 2013

antidotes.stem: A child presents after ingesting iron tablets, with persistent vomiting, hypotension, metabolic acidosis and a markedly elevated serum iron concentration.
antidotes.explain: Deferoxamine chelates circulating iron and is indicated in **severe systemic iron poisoning**, particularly with shock or metabolic acidosis.
wrong: Used for selected heavy-metal poisonings, not iron toxicity.
Used for lead poisoning, not severe iron poisoning.
antidotes.source: Royal Children’s Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline: Iron poisoning

antidotes.stem: A patient presents after a propranolol overdose with profound hypotension, bradycardia and depressed myocardial contractility despite initial resuscitation.
antidotes.explain: High-dose insulin improves myocardial energy use and contractility in severe beta-blocker poisoning; monitor **glucose and potassium** closely.
wrong: May be tried for bradycardia but is often inadequate in severe beta-blocker poisoning.
antidotes.source: AHA Focused Update on the Management of Patients With Cardiac Arrest or Life-Threatening Toxicity Due to Poisoning, 2023

antidotes.stem: A 72-year-old taking digoxin presents with vomiting, bradycardia and hypotension after an accidental overdose. ECG shows a regular wide-complex tachycardia, and serum potassium is 6.8 mmol/L.
antidotes.explain: Life-threatening dysrhythmia, **haemodynamic instability** and hyperkalaemia are indications for digoxin immune Fab.
wrong: May temporarily improve bradycardia but does not neutralise digoxin or treat the underlying toxicity.
Does not reverse digoxin toxicity; Fab is the specific treatment in this presentation.
Is not the antidote for digoxin-induced dysrhythmia or hyperkalaemia.
antidotes.source: AHA Scientific Statement: Management of Digoxin Toxicity, 2023

antidotes.stem: A patient taking lithium presents with confusion, coarse tremor and ataxia after several days of vomiting and diarrhoea. The serum lithium concentration is markedly elevated and renal function is impaired.
antidotes.explain: Severe neurological toxicity with impaired renal clearance warrants **extracorporeal treatment**, usually intermittent haemodialysis, to accelerate lithium removal.
wrong: Does not reliably enhance lithium elimination and is not the recommended extracorporeal treatment.
Is used for acetaminophen poisoning, not lithium toxicity.
antidotes.source: EXTRIP Workgroup: Recommendations for the management of lithium poisoning, 2015

antidotes.stem: A patient presents after taking a large quantity of aspirin, with tinnitus, tachypnoea and a mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis. The salicylate concentration is elevated.
antidotes.right: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate to alkalinise serum and urine
antidotes.explain: Bicarbonate-driven **urine alkalinisation** increases salicylate excretion; monitor potassium and urine pH closely.
wrong: Acidify the urine with ammonium chloride
Urine acidification increases salicylate reabsorption and worsens toxicity.
Give activated charcoal as the sole treatment
Charcoal may reduce absorption in selected patients but does not replace alkalinisation in significant poisoning.
This is not an antidote for salicylate poisoning.
antidotes.source: American College of Medical Toxicology: Guidance Document—Management Priorities in Salicylate Toxicity, 2015

antidotes.stem: A patient is brought in after ingesting a large quantity of isoniazid and develops recurrent seizures despite benzodiazepines, with severe metabolic acidosis. The amount ingested is known.
antidotes.right: Intravenous pyridoxine, gram-for-gram with the isoniazid ingested
antidotes.explain: Isoniazid depletes functional pyridoxine and impairs GABA synthesis; **pyridoxine is the specific antidote** for seizures and toxicity.
wrong: Reverses opioid toxicity, not isoniazid-induced seizures.
Is used for methotrexate toxicity, not isoniazid poisoning.
May address severe acidaemia but does not replace pyridoxine antidote therapy.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE: Isoniazid poisoning

antidotes.stem: A patient with a suspected verapamil overdose is profoundly hypotensive and bradycardic, with hyperglycaemia despite initial intravenous calcium. The patient is in intensive care.
antidotes.explain: High-dose insulin with dextrose and close glucose and potassium monitoring is a key treatment for severe **calcium-channel-blocker cardiotoxicity**.
wrong: Has a more established role in beta-blocker toxicity and is not preferred as sole treatment here.
Treat digoxin toxicity, not verapamil overdose.
Intravenous lipid emulsion as first-line therapy
Is generally reserved for selected refractory cases, not the principal initial antidotal treatment.
antidotes.source: AHA Focused Update on the Management of Patients With Cardiac Arrest or Life-Threatening Toxicity Due to Poisoning, 2023

antidotes.stem: A patient presents after a large valproate overdose with depressed consciousness, hyperammonaemia and rising liver enzymes. The valproate concentration is markedly elevated.
antidotes.explain: L-carnitine is used for significant valproate toxicity, particularly with **hyperammonaemia, hepatotoxicity or impaired consciousness**.
wrong: Is the specific antidote for isoniazid-induced seizures, not valproate toxicity.
N-acetylcysteine as the sole specific antidote
Is the antidote for acetaminophen poisoning; it does not specifically reverse valproate toxicity.
Treats muscarinic effects of cholinergic poisoning, not valproate overdose.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE: Valproate poisoning

antidotes.stem: A patient accidentally takes a large dose of methotrexate daily instead of weekly and presents with mucositis and pancytopenia. The methotrexate concentration is detectable and toxicity is suspected.
antidotes.explain: Leucovorin bypasses methotrexate’s inhibition of folate metabolism and limits toxicity; give **prompt rescue therapy** with specialist guidance.
antidotes.source: BNF: Methotrexate—management of toxicity; eviQ: Methotrexate overdose management

antidotes.stem: A patient taking apixaban presents with an intracranial haemorrhage and neurological deterioration. The last dose was taken a few hours ago.
antidotes.explain: For life-threatening or uncontrolled bleeding from apixaban, andexanet alfa is a specific reversal agent; use **urgent reversal** alongside supportive haemostatic care.
wrong: Reverses vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin, not apixaban.
antidotes.source: NICE TA697: Andexanet alfa for reversing anticoagulation from apixaban or rivaroxaban, 2021

antidotes.stem: A patient receiving an unfractionated heparin infusion develops major bleeding. The activated partial thromboplastin time is markedly prolonged and the infusion was stopped moments ago.
antidotes.explain: Protamine binds and neutralises unfractionated heparin; dose according to the **amount of heparin recently administered**.
wrong: Reverses apixaban or rivaroxaban, not heparin.
antidotes.source: BNF: Heparin—overdose and bleeding management

antidotes.stem: A laboratory worker splashes concentrated hydrofluoric acid onto a finger and develops severe deep pain with pallor despite prompt irrigation. The skin shows only a small area of erythema.
antidotes.explain: Hydrofluoric acid exposure requires decontamination followed by **calcium therapy** to bind fluoride; escalate route and monitoring according to severity.
wrong: Does not bind fluoride or treat the systemic effects of hydrofluoric acid.
Is not the specific treatment for fluoride exposure.
May reduce pain but does not neutralise fluoride or prevent tissue injury.
antidotes.source: ATSDR Medical Management Guidelines: Hydrogen Fluoride

antidotes.stem: A laboratory worker accidentally ingests an arsenic-containing pesticide and develops severe vomiting, watery diarrhoea, hypotension and a prolonged QT interval. Acute arsenic poisoning is confirmed.
antidotes.explain: For **severe acute arsenic poisoning**, give a chelating agent promptly; dimercaprol is used for serious poisoning. Consult a poison centre and provide supportive care.
wrong: Used for thallium or radioactive caesium poisoning, not arsenic.
Primarily used for severe lead poisoning.
Treats muscarinic manifestations of organophosphate poisoning, not arsenic toxicity.
antidotes.source: ATSDR Medical Management Guidelines for Arsenic; Goldfrank’s Toxicologic Emergencies, 11th ed.

antidotes.stem: A man develops painful peripheral neuropathy, abdominal symptoms and progressive hair loss after occupational exposure to a rodenticide. Testing confirms thallium poisoning.
antidotes.explain: Prussian blue binds thallium in the gut and interrupts **enterohepatic recirculation**, increasing its elimination. Give it with specialist toxicology advice.
wrong: Not the recommended antidote for thallium and may redistribute some metals.
Used for acetaminophen poisoning, not thallium.
Used for severe iron poisoning, not thallium.
antidotes.source: ATSDR Medical Management Guidelines for Thallium; WHO, Environmental Health Criteria 182: Thallium

antidotes.stem: A previously healthy adult is brought in shortly after a witnessed, isolated benzodiazepine overdose. They are deeply sedated but haemodynamically stable, with no history of chronic benzodiazepine use or seizure disorder.
antidotes.explain: In carefully selected **isolated benzodiazepine poisoning**, flumazenil can reverse sedation. Avoid it when dependence, seizures or mixed/proconvulsant overdose is possible.
wrong: Reverses opioid toxicity, not benzodiazepine effects.
May be used for selected severe anticholinergic toxicity, not benzodiazepine overdose.
Flumazenil is contraindicated in all overdoses
It is hazardous in many mixed or dependent cases, but may be considered in this carefully selected isolated ingestion.
antidotes.source: Goldfrank’s Toxicologic Emergencies, 11th ed., Benzodiazepines; AHA Focused Update on Management of Patients With Cardiac Arrest or Life-Threatening Toxicity Due to Poisoning, 2023

antidotes.stem: A patient who ingested a large quantity of diphenhydramine is delirious, flushed and dry, with mydriasis, urinary retention and sinus tachycardia. The ECG shows a narrow QRS and there is no evidence of mixed overdose.
antidotes.explain: For severe, clearly diagnosed **anticholinergic delirium**, physostigmine can reverse central and peripheral features. Use with monitoring and avoid it with QRS widening or suspected sodium-channel-blocker co-ingestion.
wrong: Reverses benzodiazepines and may provoke seizures in mixed overdoses.
Indicated for sodium-channel-blocker toxicity with QRS widening, not uncomplicated anticholinergic delirium.
antidotes.source: AHA Focused Update on Management of Patients With Cardiac Arrest or Life-Threatening Toxicity Due to Poisoning, 2023; Goldfrank’s Toxicologic Emergencies, 11th ed.

antidotes.stem: A patient with renal failure presents after a metformin overdose with shock, severe lactic acidosis and a pH of 6.8 despite initial resuscitation. The acidosis is worsening.
antidotes.explain: Severe metformin-associated lactic acidosis with **shock and profound acidemia** warrants urgent extracorporeal treatment; intermittent haemodialysis clears metformin and corrects acidosis effectively.
wrong: Used for methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning, not metformin toxicity.
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate as definitive treatment
It may be considered as a temporising measure, but does not replace extracorporeal treatment in severe poisoning.
Used for acetaminophen poisoning, not metformin-associated lactic acidosis.
antidotes.source: EXTRIP Workgroup Recommendations: Metformin; DeFronzo et al., Metformin-associated lactic acidosis, Diabetes Care 2016

antidotes.stem: A patient accidentally takes several days’ worth of 5-fluorouracil at once and presents early with severe mucositis, diarrhoea and neutropenia. The overdose is recognised within 96 hours of the end of administration.
antidotes.explain: Uridine triacetate is the specific antidote for **early, severe or life-threatening fluorouracil overdose**; start it as soon as possible, within the indicated treatment window.
wrong: Enhances fluorouracil’s antitumour effect and is not the antidote for overdose.
Does not reverse fluorouracil toxicity and may potentiate its effects.
Used to reduce toxic methotrexate concentrations in selected cases.
antidotes.source: FDA Vistogard (uridine triacetate) Prescribing Information; National Comprehensive Cancer Network, Antidote and Treatment Recommendations for 5-FU Overdose

antidotes.stem: A patient bitten by a venomous snake develops progressive ptosis, difficulty swallowing and respiratory weakness, with evidence of systemic envenoming. The species is unknown.
antidotes.explain: Antivenom is indicated for **systemic envenoming**, including neurotoxicity; administer the locally appropriate product with resuscitation and close monitoring for reactions.
wrong: May be an adjunct for some neurotoxic envenomings but does not neutralise circulating venom.
Treats organophosphate poisoning, not snake envenoming.
Do not neutralise venom or treat the underlying envenoming.
antidotes.source: WHO, Guidelines for the Management of Snakebites, 2nd ed.; WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia

antidotes.stem: A patient taking sertraline develops agitation, diaphoresis, hyperreflexia and inducible clonus after adding a serotonergic drug. Symptoms persist despite stopping the drugs and providing supportive care.
antidotes.explain: For persistent serotonin toxicity, oral cyproheptadine is a **serotonin antagonist** that may be used alongside withdrawal of serotonergic agents and supportive care.
wrong: Used for malignant hyperthermia; it is not the specific treatment for serotonin toxicity.
Used in some cases of neuroleptic malignant syndrome, not serotonin toxicity.
Used for selected anticholinergic toxicity and can be harmful in other toxidromes.
antidotes.source: Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria; Goldfrank’s Toxicologic Emergencies, 11th ed., Serotonin Syndrome

antidotes.stem: A patient with a methadone overdose initially improves after naloxone but repeatedly becomes apnoeic as the antidote wears off. They require repeated boluses to maintain adequate ventilation.
antidotes.explain: Methadone outlasts naloxone, so recurrent respiratory depression requires a **naloxone infusion**, titrated to adequate ventilation and continued with monitoring.
wrong: Reverses benzodiazepines, not opioid-induced respiratory depression.
No further antidote after the first naloxone dose
Recurrent toxicity is expected with long-acting opioids and requires continued reversal and monitoring.
antidotes.source: WHO, Community Management of Opioid Overdose; Goldfrank’s Toxicologic Emergencies, 11th ed., Opioids

antidotes.stem: A worker is found confused and hypotensive beside a fire in an enclosed industrial space. He has severe lactic acidosis and suspected cyanide exposure.
antidotes.explain: Hydroxocobalamin binds **cyanide** to form cyanocobalamin, which is excreted in urine. It is preferred in smoke-inhalation cases because it does not induce methemoglobinaemia.
wrong: Induces methemoglobinaemia and may worsen oxygen delivery in smoke-inhalation injury.
Can act as an adjunct, but is slower and is not the preferred initial antidote for severe suspected cyanide poisoning.
Treats clinically significant methemoglobinaemia, not cyanide poisoning.
antidotes.source: US FDA Cyanokit prescribing information; ATSDR Medical Management Guidelines for Cyanide

antidotes.stem: A patient is brought to the emergency department after an intentional ingestion of tuberculosis medication. He has recurrent generalised seizures that persist despite benzodiazepines and a severe metabolic acidosis.
antidotes.explain: Isoniazid depletes functionally available **pyridoxine**, impairing GABA synthesis and causing seizures. Give pyridoxine in a dose matching the estimated isoniazid dose; if unknown, give 5 g intravenously in an adult.
wrong: May be indicated for specific toxicities such as sodium-channel blockade, but it does not reverse isoniazid-induced seizures.
Used as rescue for methotrexate toxicity, not isoniazid poisoning.
Treats torsades de pointes and magnesium deficiency, not the underlying toxic seizure mechanism.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE: Isoniazid poisoning; Goldfrank’s Toxicologic Emergencies, 11th ed.

antidotes.stem: A man presents several hours after ingesting antifreeze with high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, an elevated osmolar gap and calcium oxalate crystals in his urine. Ethylene glycol poisoning is strongly suspected.
antidotes.explain: Fomepizole inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing conversion of ethylene glycol to toxic **acid metabolites**. Start treatment promptly when poisoning is suspected; do not wait for confirmatory levels.
wrong: Is the antidote for paracetamol poisoning, not ethylene glycol.
Reverses benzodiazepine effects and has no role in ethylene glycol poisoning.
Chelates iron and is used for severe iron poisoning.
antidotes.source: EXTRIP Workgroup: Ethylene glycol poisoning recommendations; fomepizole prescribing information

antidotes.stem: A patient takes a large quantity of flecainide and develops hypotension with a markedly widened QRS complex. The ECG abnormalities persist despite initial supportive care.
antidotes.explain: Sodium bicarbonate is first-line for **flecainide-induced sodium-channel blockade** and QRS widening; repeat boluses may be needed.
wrong: Useful for calcium-channel blocker toxicity, not flecainide sodium-channel blockade.
Used for torsades de pointes, not as the primary treatment for flecainide-induced QRS widening.
Reverses benzodiazepines and does not treat flecainide cardiotoxicity.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE; Goldfrank’s Toxicologic Emergencies, 11th ed.

antidotes.stem: A patient presents after taking a large amount of diltiazem, with profound hypotension, bradycardia and hyperglycaemia. Initial intravenous fluids and calcium have not restored haemodynamic stability.
antidotes.explain: High-dose insulin with glucose and close potassium monitoring is an important treatment for severe **calcium-channel blocker poisoning** with myocardial dysfunction or shock.
wrong: Glucagon is more commonly used for beta-blocker toxicity and is not the preferred definitive therapy here.
Reverses warfarin, not calcium-channel blocker toxicity.
antidotes.source: AHA Focused Update on Management of Patients With Cardiac Arrest or Life-Threatening Toxicity Due to Poisoning, 2023

antidotes.stem: A patient receiving a high-dose sodium nitroprusside infusion develops altered consciousness, severe lactic acidosis and cardiovascular collapse. Cyanide toxicity is suspected.
antidotes.explain: Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin, which can be excreted; it is a preferred antidote for **suspected cyanide toxicity**.
wrong: Used for clinically significant methaemoglobinaemia, not cyanide toxicity.
Reverses opioid toxicity, not cyanide poisoning.
Used in organophosphate poisoning, not cyanide toxicity.
antidotes.source: FDA Cyanokit (hydroxocobalamin) Prescribing Information; TOXBASE

antidotes.stem: After an overdose of a nitrate-containing medication, a patient becomes cyanotic and confused, with a low pulse-oximetry reading that does not improve with oxygen. Co-oximetry confirms significant methaemoglobinaemia.
antidotes.explain: Methylene blue reduces methaemoglobin to haemoglobin and is the specific antidotal treatment for **symptomatic acquired methaemoglobinaemia**.
wrong: An antidote for cyanide poisoning, not methaemoglobinaemia.
The antidote for paracetamol toxicity, not nitrate-associated methaemoglobinaemia.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE; British National Formulary (BNF), methaemoglobinaemia

antidotes.stem: A patient develops life-threatening intracranial bleeding shortly after receiving alteplase for an acute ischaemic stroke. The thrombolytic infusion has been stopped.
antidotes.explain: Cryoprecipitate replaces fibrinogen depleted by thrombolysis; check fibrinogen and give further replacement as guided by levels and bleeding.
antidotes.source: AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke, 2019

antidotes.stem: A patient accidentally takes a daily methotrexate dose every day for a week and develops severe mucositis and pancytopenia. The medication error is recognised promptly.
antidotes.explain: Leucovorin bypasses dihydrofolate reductase inhibition and limits cellular toxicity; start **folinic acid rescue** promptly and tailor treatment to exposure and clinical course.
wrong: Reverses warfarin anticoagulation, not methotrexate toxicity.
Used for isoniazid-associated seizures, not methotrexate toxicity.
Used for toxic alcohol poisoning, not methotrexate toxicity.
antidotes.source: BNF; TOXBASE, methotrexate poisoning

antidotes.stem: A patient taking warfarin accidentally takes several extra doses. The INR is 12, but the patient has no bleeding and is haemodynamically stable.
antidotes.explain: For a markedly raised INR without bleeding, **oral vitamin K** is used to lower the INR; urgent prothrombin complex concentrate is generally reserved for serious bleeding or urgent reversal.
wrong: Reverses factor Xa inhibitors, not warfarin.
antidotes.source: NICE NG196, Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management; BNF, warfarin

antidotes.stem: A young child is brought to the emergency department after swallowing an unknown number of iron tablets. The child has persistent vomiting, metabolic acidosis and shock.
antidotes.explain: Deferoxamine chelates iron and is indicated in severe iron poisoning, particularly with **systemic toxicity or shock**.
wrong: Treats paracetamol poisoning, not iron poisoning.
Used for selected heavy-metal poisonings and is not the antidote of choice for iron.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE, iron poisoning; BNF, deferoxamine

antidotes.stem: A patient develops major bleeding after receiving abciximab during coronary intervention. The infusion has been stopped, but bleeding continues and the platelet count is low.
antidotes.explain: Abciximab inhibits platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa; platelet transfusion can provide **functional platelets** in severe or life-threatening bleeding.
wrong: Reverses vitamin K antagonists, not abciximab.
antidotes.source: ReoPro (abciximab) Prescribing Information; BNF, abciximab

antidotes.stem: A toddler is brought in several hours after swallowing an unknown number of ferrous sulfate tablets. They have repeated vomiting, abdominal pain and metabolic acidosis, with a markedly elevated serum iron concentration.
antidotes.explain: Deferoxamine chelates iron in **severe acute iron poisoning**; systemic toxicity and metabolic acidosis are indications for treatment.
wrong: Used for paracetamol poisoning, not iron
Does not chelate iron or treat systemic iron toxicity
Iron is poorly adsorbed by activated charcoal
antidotes.source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline: Iron poisoning

antidotes.stem: A patient presents after a deliberate aspirin overdose with tinnitus, tachypnoea and a raised salicylate concentration. They are alert, and renal function is adequate.
antidotes.right: IV sodium bicarbonate to alkalinise urine
antidotes.explain: Urinary alkalinisation with IV bicarbonate increases **salicylate excretion**; monitor urine pH and correct hypokalaemia.
wrong: Activated charcoal as the sole treatment
May reduce absorption early but does not treat established salicylate toxicity
antidotes.source: American College of Medical Toxicology: Guidance Document on the Management Priorities in Salicylate Toxicity (2015)

antidotes.stem: After taking a large quantity of sotalol, a patient develops recurrent episodes of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a prolonged QT interval. The episodes persist despite correction of hypoxia and electrolytes.
antidotes.explain: Torsades de pointes is treated acutely with **IV magnesium**, even if the serum magnesium concentration is normal; overdrive pacing may be needed if it recurs.
wrong: Does not treat torsades and may delay definitive management
Can worsen hypotension and does not terminate torsades
Does not treat torsades and may provoke arrhythmias
antidotes.source: AHA Focused Update on the Management of Patients With Cardiac Arrest or Life-Threatening Toxicity Due to Poisoning (2023)

antidotes.stem: A patient is brought in after a quinidine overdose with hypotension and a markedly widened QRS complex on ECG. There is no evidence of torsades de pointes.
antidotes.explain: Quinidine can cause **cardiac sodium-channel blockade**; IV bicarbonate is used for QRS widening and associated haemodynamic toxicity.
wrong: Does not treat toxic QRS widening
antidotes.source: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11th ed.: Sodium Channel Blocker Toxicity

antidotes.stem: During a regional nerve block with bupivacaine, a patient develops a seizure followed by ventricular arrhythmia and cardiovascular collapse. Standard resuscitation measures are being started.
antidotes.explain: This is **local anaesthetic systemic toxicity**; administer 20% lipid emulsion promptly alongside modified resuscitation.
wrong: Used for methaemoglobinaemia, not local anaesthetic cardiotoxicity
Reverses opioid toxicity, not bupivacaine toxicity
Reverses benzodiazepines and is not an antidote for bupivacaine
antidotes.source: American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine: Checklist for Treatment of Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (2020)

antidotes.stem: A patient presents after swallowing a large number of potassium chloride tablets. They are weak, and the ECG shows tall peaked T waves with progressive QRS widening; serum potassium is markedly elevated.
antidotes.explain: IV calcium rapidly stabilises the myocardium in **hyperkalaemic ECG changes**; additional measures are needed to lower serum potassium.
wrong: Does not stabilise the myocardium in hyperkalaemia
antidotes.source: Resuscitation Council UK: Emergency Treatment of Hyperkalaemia (2021)

antidotes.stem: A patient with diabetes is found confused after injecting far more insulin than prescribed. Their blood glucose is 1.8 mmol/L, and hypoglycaemia recurs after an initial glucose bolus.
antidotes.right: IV dextrose followed by a titrated dextrose infusion
antidotes.explain: Treat severe insulin-induced hypoglycaemia with **IV glucose**, then continue glucose and frequent monitoring because the effect of the insulin may be prolonged.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE: Insulin poisoning

antidotes.stem: A patient presents after an acute oral amiodarone overdose with bradycardia and hypotension. They have no torsades de pointes, and the airway and circulation are being supported.
antidotes.right: Supportive care with continuous cardiac monitoring
antidotes.explain: There is **no specific antidote** for amiodarone overdose; management is supportive and directed at the resulting bradycardia, hypotension or arrhythmia.
wrong: Indicated for life-threatening digoxin toxicity, not amiodarone
antidotes.source: Poisons Information Monograph: Amiodarone (TOXBASE)

antidotes.stem: A patient who accidentally ingested a large quantity of ivabradine presents with symptomatic sinus bradycardia and hypotension. There is no evidence of another co-ingestant.
antidotes.right: Atropine for symptomatic bradycardia, with supportive care
antidotes.explain: Ivabradine overdose has **no specific antidote**; manage symptomatic bradycardia with standard supportive measures, including atropine when appropriate.
wrong: Treats iron poisoning, not ivabradine toxicity
antidotes.source: European Medicines Agency: Procoralan (ivabradine) Summary of Product Characteristics

antidotes.stem: A patient presents after taking a very large quantity of atorvastatin and has severe muscle pain, a markedly elevated creatine kinase concentration and myoglobinuria. Renal function is currently preserved.
antidotes.right: IV isotonic crystalloid with monitoring for renal injury
antidotes.explain: Statin-associated rhabdomyolysis is managed with **supportive care and IV fluids** to reduce the risk of acute kidney injury; there is no specific antidote.
wrong: Chelates iron and does not treat rhabdomyolysis
IV sodium bicarbonate as a specific antidote
It is not an antidote for statin poisoning; fluids and monitoring are central
antidotes.source: BNF: Statins—management of adverse effects; TOXBASE: Statins

antidotes.stem: A patient with renal impairment accidentally receives several therapeutic doses of enoxaparin and develops major gastrointestinal bleeding. The last dose was given two hours ago.
antidotes.explain: Protamine **partially reverses** enoxaparin’s anticoagulant effect, particularly its anti-IIa activity. Reversal is incomplete for anti-Xa activity.
wrong: Reverses vitamin K antagonists, not low-molecular-weight heparin.
antidotes.source: ASH 2018 guidelines for management of venous thromboembolism: optimal management of anticoagulation therapy

antidotes.stem: A patient is brought in after taking a large amount of clonidine and is deeply drowsy, bradycardic and hypotensive. Airway and breathing are currently maintained.
antidotes.explain: There is **no specific antidote**; supportive airway and circulatory care are central. High-dose naloxone may be tried for significant CNS depression, but response is variable.
wrong: May be considered for symptomatic bradycardia but does not reverse the overall toxicity.
Is not an antidote for clonidine poisoning.
antidotes.source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline: Clonidine poisoning

antidotes.stem: A patient takes a large amount of lisinopril and develops persistent hypotension despite an initial crystalloid bolus. There is no angioedema or evidence of another co-ingestion.
antidotes.explain: ACE-inhibitor overdose has **no specific antidote**; treat hypotension with fluids and, if needed, vasopressors such as norepinephrine.
wrong: Used in selected beta-blocker poisonings, not ACE-inhibitor overdose.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE: Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs) poisoning

antidotes.stem: After a procainamide overdose, a patient develops hypotension, ventricular arrhythmia and marked QRS widening on the ECG.
antidotes.explain: Procainamide can cause **cardiac sodium-channel blockade** and QRS widening. Give sodium bicarbonate and manage the patient with toxicology and critical-care support.
wrong: Is not the specific treatment for sodium-channel-blocker cardiotoxicity.
antidotes.source: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11th ed.: Sodium Channel Blocker Toxicity

antidotes.stem: A patient presents after a substantial theophylline overdose with persistent vomiting, tachyarrhythmia and a markedly elevated serum concentration despite initial supportive treatment.
antidotes.explain: Theophylline is dialysable; extracorporeal treatment is recommended for **severe poisoning** or serious clinical features, with intermittent haemodialysis preferred when available.
wrong: Is the antidote for paracetamol poisoning, not theophylline.
antidotes.source: EXTRIP Workgroup: Theophylline recommendations

antidotes.stem: A patient develops life-threatening bleeding during an eptifibatide infusion for acute coronary syndrome. The infusion is stopped, but bleeding continues.
antidotes.explain: Eptifibatide reversibly inhibits platelet GP IIb/IIIa receptors; platelet transfusion can provide functional platelets, particularly after the drug has cleared from plasma.
wrong: Reverses vitamin K antagonists, not eptifibatide.
antidotes.source: BNF: Eptifibatide; prescribing information for eptifibatide

antidotes.stem: A patient takes a large overdose of ticagrelor and develops major bleeding. There is no locally available specific reversal agent.
antidotes.right: Stop ticagrelor and provide supportive haemostatic care
antidotes.explain: There is **no routinely available specific antidote** in this setting. Platelet transfusion may be ineffective soon after ingestion because circulating ticagrelor can inhibit transfused platelets.
antidotes.source: BNF: Ticagrelor; European Heart Journal 2022: Management of bleeding and procedures in patients on oral antithrombotic treatment

antidotes.stem: A patient presents after swallowing a large quantity of oral minoxidil and has profound hypotension with reflex tachycardia. Initial intravenous fluids have not restored blood pressure.
antidotes.explain: Minoxidil overdose causes severe vasodilation; treatment is **supportive**, using fluids and vasopressors for persistent hypotension. There is no specific antidote.
wrong: May be tried in some clonidine poisonings but does not reverse minoxidil toxicity.
Is not a specific treatment for minoxidil-induced vasodilatory shock.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE: Minoxidil poisoning

antidotes.stem: A patient receiving a tirofiban infusion develops major bleeding during coronary intervention. The infusion is stopped and the patient remains haemodynamically stable.
antidotes.right: Discontinue tirofiban and provide supportive care
antidotes.explain: Tirofiban’s antiplatelet effect is **reversible and short-lived**; stopping the infusion is the key step, with blood products or other support guided by the bleeding.
wrong: Reverses vitamin K antagonists, not tirofiban.
antidotes.source: BNF: Tirofiban; tirofiban Summary of Product Characteristics

antidotes.stem: A patient receiving an intravenous amiodarone infusion develops a painful, erythematous swelling at the cannula site after extravasation. The infusion has been stopped.
antidotes.explain: Hyaluronidase is used as an **extravasation treatment** to facilitate dispersion and absorption of the infiltrated drug; follow local extravasation guidance and provide supportive care.
antidotes.source: Royal College of Nursing: Management of extravasation injuries; local medicines extravasation guidance

antidotes.stem: A patient presents after a large atenolol overdose with marked bradycardia and hypotension despite initial fluid resuscitation. There is no evidence of hypoglycaemia.
antidotes.explain: Glucagon increases intracellular cAMP **independently of beta receptors** and is an initial antidotal treatment for severe beta-blocker toxicity; high-dose insulin may also be required.
wrong: Atropine may be tried but often does not reverse severe beta-blocker toxicity.
Calcium is used for calcium-channel blocker toxicity, not as the specific treatment for beta-blocker overdose.
This is used for sodium-channel blockade with QRS widening, not isolated beta-blocker toxicity.
antidotes.source: AHA Focused Update on the Management of Patients With Cardiac Arrest or Life-Threatening Toxicity Due to Poisoning, 2023

antidotes.stem: A patient takes a large overdose of doxazosin and develops profound hypotension with warm peripheries. Fluid resuscitation has not restored the blood pressure.
antidotes.explain: Alpha-1 blockade causes vasodilatory hypotension; use **vasopressor support**, typically norepinephrine, if fluids are inadequate.
wrong: Glucagon is used principally for severe beta-blocker toxicity.
This is an antidote for life-threatening digoxin toxicity, not alpha-blocker poisoning.
Protamine reverses heparin anticoagulation and does not treat doxazosin toxicity.
antidotes.source: Goldfrank’s Toxicologic Emergencies, 11th ed.

antidotes.stem: A patient presents after ingesting a large amount of hydralazine and remains severely hypotensive despite intravenous fluids. There is no evidence of haemorrhage.
antidotes.explain: Hydralazine overdose can cause marked **arteriolar vasodilation and hypotension**; persistent shock is managed with vasopressors such as norepinephrine.
wrong: Vitamin K reverses vitamin K antagonist anticoagulation, not hydralazine-induced vasodilation.
Glucagon is used for beta-blocker toxicity and is not the specific treatment here.
Methylene blue is used for selected causes of methaemoglobinaemia or refractory vasoplegia, not as routine hydralazine overdose treatment.
antidotes.source: Goldfrank’s Toxicologic Emergencies, 11th ed.

antidotes.stem: A patient taking a massive clopidogrel overdose develops life-threatening gastrointestinal bleeding despite local haemostatic measures. The last dose was taken several hours ago.
antidotes.explain: For life-threatening bleeding with clopidogrel-associated platelet dysfunction, **platelet transfusion** may provide functional platelets; benefit can be limited soon after dosing because active metabolite may inhibit transfused platelets.
wrong: Idarucizumab specifically reverses dabigatran, not clopidogrel.
Vitamin K reverses warfarin and does not reverse P2Y12 inhibition.
Protamine reverses heparin, not clopidogrel-associated platelet inhibition.
antidotes.source: BSH Guidelines on the Use of Antiplatelet Drugs in Haematology, 2019

antidotes.stem: A patient taking edoxaban presents with life-threatening intracranial haemorrhage. Edoxaban-specific reversal is unavailable locally.
antidotes.explain: When a specific reversal agent is unavailable, **4-factor PCC** is recommended for life-threatening factor Xa inhibitor-associated bleeding; it does not remove edoxaban from the circulation.
wrong: Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor.
Protamine reverses unfractionated heparin and only partially reverses some low-molecular-weight heparins.
Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not direct factor Xa inhibitors.
antidotes.source: European Heart Rhythm Association Practical Guide on the Use of Non-Vitamin K Antagonist Oral Anticoagulants, 2021

antidotes.stem: A patient presents after a large hydroxychloroquine overdose with hypotension, QRS widening and ventricular dysrhythmia. The patient is also profoundly hypokalaemic.
antidotes.explain: Severe hydroxychloroquine poisoning is treated with **early epinephrine** for hypotension, alongside supportive toxicology care; carefully correct hypokalaemia and monitor the ECG.
wrong: Vitamin K reverses vitamin K antagonist anticoagulants and has no role in hydroxychloroquine toxicity.
Protamine is used to reverse heparin anticoagulation.
This treats severe digoxin toxicity, not hydroxychloroquine overdose.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE: Hydroxychloroquine poisoning

antidotes.stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease takes a large spironolactone overdose and presents with potassium 7.2 mmol/L and broad, peaked T waves on ECG.
antidotes.explain: With ECG changes, give intravenous calcium to **stabilise the cardiac membrane immediately**; insulin with glucose and other measures are also needed to lower serum potassium.
wrong: It acts too slowly to stabilise the myocardium in life-threatening hyperkalaemia.
Vitamin K reverses warfarin and does not treat hyperkalaemia.
Protamine reverses heparin and has no role in spironolactone-associated hyperkalaemia.
antidotes.source: UK Kidney Association Clinical Practice Guideline: Management of Hyperkalaemia in Adults, 2023

antidotes.stem: A patient takes a large bumetanide overdose and develops severe hypokalaemia with muscle weakness and ventricular ectopy. Renal function is preserved and there are no ECG features of hyperkalaemia.
antidotes.explain: Severe symptomatic hypokalaemia with arrhythmia requires **urgent potassium replacement**, with ECG monitoring and repeat electrolyte measurement.
wrong: Calcium is used to stabilise the myocardium in hyperkalaemia, not to correct hypokalaemia.
Bicarbonate can worsen hypokalaemia by shifting potassium intracellularly.
Insulin shifts potassium into cells and would worsen the hypokalaemia.
antidotes.source: NICE Clinical Knowledge Summary: Hypokalaemia

antidotes.stem: A patient presents after taking a large overdose of cilostazol and develops persistent tachycardia, flushing and hypotension. There is no major haemorrhage or specific antidote available.
antidotes.right: Supportive care with intravenous fluids and monitoring
antidotes.explain: There is **no specific antidote** for cilostazol overdose; management is supportive, including haemodynamic support and observation for bleeding or cardiac effects.
wrong: Vitamin K reverses warfarin and does not counter cilostazol’s antiplatelet effects.
Protamine reverses heparin and does not reverse cilostazol.
antidotes.source: BNF: Cilostazol; product information and overdose guidance

antidotes.stem: A patient accidentally receives a prolonged adenosine infusion and develops persistent high-grade AV block with hypotension. The infusion has been stopped, but the block continues.
antidotes.explain: Aminophylline antagonises adenosine receptors and can reverse persistent adenosine effects; provide **supportive care** and pacing if required.
wrong: May be used for symptomatic bradycardia, but it does not directly antagonise adenosine.
Used for severe digoxin toxicity, not adenosine toxicity.
Used in selected beta-blocker poisoning, not adenosine toxicity.
antidotes.source: Adenosine injection prescribing information; AHA ACLS bradycardia guidance

antidotes.stem: A patient receives a large intravenous milrinone overdose and develops profound hypotension with a rapid atrial arrhythmia. There is no evidence of anaphylaxis or another cause of shock.
antidotes.right: Stop milrinone and give haemodynamic support with a vasopressor
antidotes.explain: There is **no specific antidote** for milrinone toxicity; stop the infusion and support perfusion, typically with a vasopressor, while managing the arrhythmia.
wrong: May be used in beta-blocker poisoning, not phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor toxicity.
Treats life-threatening digoxin toxicity, not milrinone overdose.
antidotes.source: Milrinone lactate injection prescribing information; TOXBASE, Milrinone

antidotes.stem: A patient receiving an argatroban infusion is accidentally given a tenfold overdose and develops major gastrointestinal bleeding. The infusion is stopped, but the anticoagulant effect persists while the drug clears.
antidotes.right: Stop argatroban and provide supportive haemostatic care; there is no specific antidote.
antidotes.explain: Argatroban has **no specific reversal agent**. Its short half-life means anticoagulant activity usually falls after stopping the infusion; manage bleeding supportively.
wrong: Reverses heparin, not the direct thrombin inhibitor argatroban.
Reverses vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin, not argatroban.
antidotes.source: Argatroban prescribing information; BNF, Argatroban

antidotes.stem: A patient taking rivaroxaban presents with a life-threatening intracranial haemorrhage after an accidental overdose. The last dose was taken recently and a specific reversal agent is available.
antidotes.explain: Andexanet alfa is a **specific reversal agent** for rivaroxaban and apixaban. It is used for life-threatening or uncontrolled bleeding associated with these factor Xa inhibitors.
wrong: Reverses dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor.
Reverses unfractionated heparin and partially reverses low-molecular-weight heparin.
Reverses vitamin K antagonists, not rivaroxaban.
antidotes.source: NICE TA697; BNF, Andexanet alfa

antidotes.stem: A patient taking empagliflozin presents after an overdose with nausea, deep breathing and a high-anion-gap acidosis; glucose is 9 mmol/L and serum ketones are markedly elevated.
antidotes.explain: This is **euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis**. Give insulin to suppress ketogenesis while providing dextrose to prevent hypoglycaemia.
wrong: Not routine treatment for DKA; it does not stop ketogenesis.
Inadequate for significant DKA with acidosis.
Raises glucose but does not treat the ketoacidosis.
antidotes.source: Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults

antidotes.stem: A patient presents after drinking antifreeze with confusion, high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, hypocalcaemia and calcium oxalate crystals in the urine.
antidotes.explain: Fomepizole inhibits **alcohol dehydrogenase**, preventing formation of toxic ethylene glycol metabolites. Severe poisoning may also require haemodialysis.
wrong: Used for acetaminophen poisoning, not ethylene glycol.
Reverses benzodiazepines and does not block ethylene glycol metabolism.
Used for some cases of methaemoglobinaemia, not ethylene glycol poisoning.
antidotes.source: EXTRIP Workgroup, Ethylene Glycol Recommendations; fomepizole prescribing information

antidotes.stem: A patient develops blurred vision and severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis after ingesting illicit spirits; testing shows an elevated methanol concentration.
antidotes.explain: Fomepizole blocks **alcohol dehydrogenase**, limiting production of formic acid, the metabolite responsible for visual and systemic toxicity. Severe poisoning may also need haemodialysis.
wrong: Ethanol can block alcohol dehydrogenase, but fomepizole is preferred when available because it is more predictable.
Reverses opioid toxicity, not methanol poisoning.
Used for organophosphate poisoning, not methanol.
antidotes.source: EXTRIP Workgroup, Methanol Recommendations; fomepizole prescribing information

antidotes.stem: After a large valproate ingestion, a patient becomes drowsy and develops hyperammonaemia; liver enzymes are only mildly elevated.
antidotes.explain: Valproate can deplete carnitine and cause **hyperammonaemic encephalopathy**. Give IV L-carnitine in significant poisoning, particularly with encephalopathy or hyperammonaemia.
wrong: Used for isoniazid-induced seizures, not valproate toxicity.
Used for methotrexate toxicity, not valproate-associated hyperammonaemia.
May be indicated for coagulopathy, but does not treat valproate-associated hyperammonaemia.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE, Sodium valproate poisoning; American Association of Poison Control Centers consensus guideline for valproate poisoning

antidotes.stem: A patient presents after a large amlodipine overdose with profound hypotension, bradycardia and hyperglycaemia despite intravenous calcium and vasopressors.
antidotes.explain: High-dose insulin improves myocardial carbohydrate utilisation and contractility in severe **calcium-channel blocker poisoning**; give dextrose and monitor potassium closely.
wrong: Used for sulfonylurea-associated hypoglycaemia, not calcium-channel blocker shock.
May have limited effect and does not address severe cardiogenic shock.
antidotes.source: American Heart Association, Focused Update on the Management of Patients With Cardiac Arrest or Life-Threatening Toxicity Due to Poisoning, 2023

antidotes.stem: Following a propranolol overdose, a patient develops seizures, hypotension, bradycardia and a widened QRS complex.
antidotes.explain: Propranolol can cause **fast sodium-channel blockade** with QRS widening; IV sodium bicarbonate is indicated for this cardiotoxicity. Treat other manifestations concurrently.
wrong: Primarily used for calcium-channel blocker toxicity or membrane stabilisation in hyperkalaemia.
Used for selected cases of methaemoglobinaemia or vasoplegia, not propranolol-induced QRS widening.
antidotes.source: AHA, Focused Update on the Management of Patients With Cardiac Arrest or Life-Threatening Toxicity Due to Poisoning, 2023; TOXBASE, Propranolol poisoning

antidotes.stem: A worker collapses after an enclosed-space fire and has severe lactic acidosis, hypotension and altered consciousness, raising strong suspicion of cyanide poisoning.
antidotes.explain: Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide to form **cyanocobalamin**, which is excreted in urine. Do not delay treatment for a cyanide level in a critically ill patient.
wrong: Can cause methaemoglobinaemia and is less suitable when smoke inhalation and carbon monoxide exposure are possible.
Used for significant muscarinic features of cholinergic poisoning.
Treats methaemoglobinaemia but does not bind cyanide.
antidotes.source: American Heart Association, Focused Update on the Management of Patients With Cardiac Arrest or Life-Threatening Toxicity Due to Poisoning, 2023; Cyanokit prescribing information

antidotes.stem: A patient presents several hours after a deliberate acetaminophen overdose; the timed serum concentration is above the treatment line on the nomogram.
antidotes.explain: N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and detoxifies the reactive metabolite **NAPQI**, reducing the risk of hepatic injury.
wrong: An antidote for methanol and ethylene glycol; not standard first-line treatment for acetaminophen overdose.
Used in selected cases of valproate toxicity, not acetaminophen overdose.
antidotes.source: NICE Clinical Knowledge Summary, Management of poisoning: acetaminophen; TOXBASE, Paracetamol poisoning

antidotes.stem: After ingesting an industrial fluoride-containing product, a patient develops perioral tingling, tetany, QT prolongation and severe hypocalcaemia.
antidotes.explain: Fluoride binds calcium and can cause life-threatening **hypocalcaemia** and cardiac instability. IV calcium gluconate treats the acute electrolyte disturbance.
wrong: Used for selected sodium-channel-blocking drug overdoses, not fluoride-induced hypocalcaemia.
Does not correct the severe calcium deficit.
Chelates iron and does not treat fluoride poisoning.
antidotes.source: ATSDR, Medical Management Guidelines for Hydrogen Fluoride; TOXBASE, Fluoride poisoning
